title: Correctness & Coordination
summary: Getting the right answer when parts fail independently. 6 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Idempotency — Making a repeated operation produce the same result as one execution, usually via a client-supplied key recorded with the effect.
Saga — A multi-step workflow across services where each step has a compensating action, because no distributed transaction is available.
Reservation / Hold — Temporarily claiming a scarce resource with an expiry, so a user can complete a multi-step flow without it being sold underneath them.
Conflict Resolution — Deciding what the truth is when two writers modified the same thing concurrently — last-write-wins, version vectors, OT or CRDTs.
Leader Election — Picking exactly one node to perform a role, with an agreed way to notice failure and pick again.
Distributed Lock — A lease held in a shared store that grants one holder the right to act on a resource for a bounded time.

questions.prompt: Idempotency vs Exactly-Once (Effectively-Once) vs Reservation / Hold — what decides between them?
points: Exactly-Once (Effectively-Once) — The pipeline-level version of the same goal; idempotency is the per-operation building block.
Reservation / Hold — When the operation must hold a scarce resource rather than just be safe to repeat.
Idempotency — Making a repeated operation produce the same result as one execution, usually via a client-supplied key recorded with the effect.
questions.answer: Exactly-Once (Effectively-Once): The pipeline-level version of the same goal; idempotency is the per-operation building block. Reservation / Hold: When the operation must hold a scarce resource rather than just be safe to repeat.

questions.prompt: Idempotency appears in 9 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Notification System — Deduplicates sends, so an at-least-once redelivery does not mean the user's phone buzzes twice for one event.
Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger) — The client-supplied key on every transfer, recorded in the same transaction as the ledger entry — the difference between a retry and a double charge.
Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — Booking requests carry a key, so a double-tap or a lost response does not leave one user holding two seats for the same show.
Design a Prescription Drug Marketplace — Orders must survive retry without dispensing twice; the key is recorded with the fulfilment record, not before it.
Design a Distributed Job Scheduler — A job execution is keyed, so at-least-once dispatch does not run the same scheduled task twice on two different workers.
Design a Webhook Delivery System — The delivery id sent with every request, so receivers can recognise a redelivery. Its absence is what makes at-least-once dangerous for them.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — Token issuance and refresh are made repeat-safe, so a retried login does not mint a second live session the user cannot see or revoke.

Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — A redelivered alert file must not re-investigate what was already decided, so the key is the source alert id and revision rather than anything the pipeline generates.

Design a Business Verification Pipeline — A vendor timeout is ambiguous about whether the work happened, so the retry has to record one result and incur one charge no matter how many attempts it took.

Its absence is what makes at-least-once dangerous for them. in Design an Authentication & Session Service, token issuance and refresh are made repeat-safe, so a retried login does not mint a second live session the user cannot see or revoke. in Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System, a redelivered alert file must not re-investigate what was already decided, so the key is the source alert id and revision rather than anything the pipeline generates. in Design a Business Verification Pipeline, a vendor timeout is ambiguous about whether the work happened, so the retry has to record one result and incur one charge no matter how many attempts it took.

questions.prompt: Reservation / Hold vs Distributed Lock vs Saga — what decides between them?
points: Distributed Lock — A lock blocks others outright; a reservation is a lock with an owner, an expiry and a business meaning.
Saga — When the hold spans several services, the reservation becomes one step of a saga.
Reservation / Hold — Temporarily claiming a scarce resource with an expiry, so a user can complete a multi-step flow without it being sold underneath them.
questions.answer: Distributed Lock: A lock blocks others outright; a reservation is a lock with an owner, an expiry and a business meaning. Saga: When the hold spans several services, the reservation becomes one step of a saga.

questions.prompt: Reservation / Hold appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Ride-Sharing Service — A driver is held for a rider while the offer is outstanding, so two riders cannot be matched to the same car.
Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — Seats are held for the duration of checkout with an expiry — the mechanism that prevents overselling without locking for the whole session.
Design a Prescription Drug Marketplace — Stock is held while the order and its authorisation clear, since dispensing against inventory that is already gone is not recoverable.

Design a Human Review Queue — A claimed item is held under an expiring lease, which gives at-most-one-active-reviewer without a lock service and returns the item automatically when someone closes their laptop.

questions.prompt: Conflict Resolution vs Message Ordering vs Distributed Lock — what decides between them?
points: Message Ordering — Route all writes for one key through one partition and the conflict never arises.
Distributed Lock — Prevent concurrent modification instead of reconciling it — at the cost of availability.
Conflict Resolution — Deciding what the truth is when two writers modified the same thing concurrently — last-write-wins, version vectors, OT or CRDTs.
questions.answer: Message Ordering: Route all writes for one key through one partition and the conflict never arises. Distributed Lock: Prevent concurrent modification instead of reconciling it — at the cost of availability.

questions.prompt: Conflict Resolution appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Collaborative Document Editor — Concurrent edits to the same region are merged rather than rejected — the decision that makes collaborative editing feel live instead of contested.
Design a File Sync / Object Storage Service — Two devices editing the same file offline produce divergent versions, and the design must choose between merging and conflicted copies.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — Concurrent writes accepted by different replicas are reconciled with version vectors, since a quorum permits them by construction.

Design a Business Verification Pipeline — The document, the registry and the applicant will state different addresses, so precedence is declared in advance and the winning source is recorded rather than silently overwriting.

questions.prompt: Distributed Lock vs Idempotency vs Message Ordering — what decides between them?
points: Idempotency — Make the double execution harmless instead of preventing it. Fewer moving parts, no TTL to tune.
Message Ordering — Serialise by routing to one partition owner rather than by contending on a lock.
Distributed Lock — A lease held in a shared store that grants one holder the right to act on a resource for a bounded time.
questions.answer: Idempotency: Make the double execution harmless instead of preventing it. Fewer moving parts, no TTL to tune. Message Ordering: Serialise by routing to one partition owner rather than by contending on a lock.

questions.prompt: Distributed Lock appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.

Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — Guards the seat-hold critical section under flash-sale contention, where optimistic retry alone would thrash.
Design a Distributed Job Scheduler — Ensures one scheduler tick executes once, with a lease so a crashed holder does not stall the schedule forever.
